text: she had come back to the house but even, she realized, when she thought she was out of reach of the noise, the death rattle, the power¬ ful bellows that reached her now through the ceiling, or perhaps down the stairway and through the vestibule, passing through two doors, arriving, muffled but distinct, 112 like the regular and terrible pulsations of some organ in¬ stalled at the very center of the house, as if the woman it emanated from was lying in a kind of royal solitude, ceremonious and solemn, to which not only the loss of her faculties, her inability to communicate, relegated her, but even more the terrible grandeur of the action she was en¬ gaged in, the act of dying—, like those queens universally abandoned at the same time that they are the object of everyone's morbid, voracious, and fascinated curiosity, forced by a barbarous and pitiless protocol to give birth and to die in public: henceforth no longer a simple, nat¬ ural act, but a ceremonial, a rite; and during that moment Louise had reached for the tureen on the hot-plate, had helped herself, and was eating now, that is, her throat was docilely swallowing one after another the spoonsful of the warm and opaque liquid having not so much a flavor, a taste, as the quality of a particular substance— slightly grainy—which her palate and her tongue were content to register without transmitting anything to the higher echelons of consciousness, her mind entirely occu¬ pied with wondering if she could escape, even if only for a moment (since even at the foot of the hill, near the wall, face to face with the cat, and later too, she hadn't been able to) that noise, and not only now but later (since it wasn't even necessary for her ears to hear it), then (the old man must have raised his voice, or rather it must have been the quality of the silence that followed—outraged, suffocating, even before Sabine answered—which became 113 louder, for actually he had not raised his voice, not even raised his eyes to look at her, merely saying between two spoonsful of soup and in a calm, impersonal tone—-and with more lassitude than acrimony, and more exhaustion than mockery, and more resignation than exasperation in his voice: “Maybe you'd better ask for their shit to look through. Isn't that what the newspapers say they do with those Negroes?") Sabine looked at the old man's face, or at least what she could see of it, for he was already leaning over his plate again while the silence grew heavier, Sabine motionless, mouth open—although her plate was empty and the spoon still lying beside it (plate and spoon useless but still set at her place each evening for the last twenty years, since the reading of that famous reducing article, probably out of obedience to a kind of protocol, as if it were tacitly understood, agreed, decided upon among the servants, the succession of female domestics whose duty it was to set the table, that they should pre¬ tend not to notice (servants not being supposed to know such things) that she no longer ate soup, that is, that she was getting fat, that is—since putting on weight was a particular function of age—that she was growing old), mouth open, then, as if she too were trying to swallow something (perhaps merely the air, nothing but the in¬ visible air which had served as a vehicle for the words, the invisible words which had passed through it without leaving any traces behind, by means of infinitesimal com¬ pressions and decompressions, leaving it intact, ready to 114 be used again, a subtle, dangerous, enigmatic and trans¬ parent messenger, thought—words—having no need, as on paper, to take shape, assume form, materialize there by means of lines, apparent and durable signs, but borrowing the air as, so to speak, the fish borrows water: a simple quiver, a mere vibration, an undulation, a flash, the shim¬ mer of a silvery underside, green over blue, the deceived fisherman still imagining he sees the trout long since escaped, peering, his eyes squinting, holding his breath so as not to frighten but to surprise, to catch the imma¬ terial, the ineffable reflection of light on the pebbles, the sand, or the weeds of the bottom: nothing) and finally managing to say: “I should ... You said I should .. ” Then her voice stopped. Not that she refused to pro¬ nounce, to repeat the same words, the gibe, the insult, but because he (the old man sitting opposite her) obviously wasn’t listening to her any more, although he was still staring in her direction (her back was to the door), his spoon again stopped half way between the plate and his mouth, but his eyes passing over her head now, fixed on something—or someone—she didn’t see, probably behind her, and when she turned around she saw him too, no longer behind her now but to her left passing silently along the sideboard, passing into the lamplit area: the lean body, the face lean too and not tanned but apparently blackened or rather soiled by the sun, as if covered with a layer of greasepaint, like people who make up as Negroes for Mardi Gras, not dark, then, but soiled, and perhaps even 115 with grease on one of the bony cheeks and across the fore¬ head, soiling the light hair scarcely distinguishable—with the spots, the grease—from the dark skin, the forearms below the rolled-up sleeves darkened by the same sun that had bleached their blond hairs and by the grease too, and spread now on each side of the plate, the upper part of the body in the stained overalls leaning forward now, the head almost resting on the plate, the chin almost touching the edge, so that the bony, delicate hand holding the spoon traversed, at each rise and fall, only a minimum circuit (sitting down, helping himself without a word, eating now with that kind of concentration, that taciturn and methodical greed of the peasants, the old man’s stare still riveted on him), and after a moment the old man seeming to remember his own spoon, completing the unfinished gesture, he too raising the spoon to his mouth and swallowing, as if it were beneath his notice, his eyes not leaving Georges for a moment, and the hand lowering, setting the spoon down again in what remained of the soup but staying down this time, not rising again, the eyes still fixed on the head of which only the blond hair could be seen, hanging almost into the plate, and behind it the spoon continuing its methodical oscillation, and then Sabine hurriedly clearing her throat and saying: “Pierre . . but the fat man not moving, enormous, pachy- dermous, still staring at Georges, and Sabine again: “Pierre, please, you know . . 116 "Know what?” Georges asked. And Sabine: "Nothing. Your father . . And Georges: "What’s the matter?” And Sabine: "Your father ... I mean we ... I mean, I was worried, I was wondering what you . . .” And Georges: "The pump broke down. It’s not my fault if all the equipment on this damn place is falling to pieces . . .” She would remember that: that evening (or perhaps another, one of those ten dinners, one of those ten days it took the old woman to manage, to be entitled, finally, to die), thinking (Louise) about all it took to make not a man or a woman, but a corpse—one of those things wrapped up in water-tight boxes and then buried in the ground under conditions and at a depth regulated with a view to protecting the population against the risk of epidemics that might result from the decomposition, the rotting of bodies, carrion, and other rubbish—and not only ten days—or three, or six, it didn’t matter—-of agony, but the total of months, of years, of dawns, of evenings, of nights, of food digested, of clothes worn, worn out: the terrible accumulation, addition, enumeration kept day by day with the monotonous repetition of the fateful rubrics "Debits,” "Credits,” all in the same correct, impersonal, inflexible, and modest handwriting that entered, v/ithout indicating (without allowing itself to indicate) any differ¬ ence, shoes resoled, gas-meter readings, and the slight or 117 irremediable disasters (The Martin bill for digging out the part of the cellar that collapsed 83 hours of work @ 2 Fr. an hour makes 166 Fr., Martin owed us 146 Fr. on the 600 we lent him, we owe him 20 Fr. Two balls darning cotton 3 Fr. 20. Beginning of our father's sickness. Bicycle license 18 Fr. Whitewashing the garden front 645 Fr. Six dozen eggs put up at 5 Fr. 25 makes 31 Fr. 50. Medications (wine and pills) 20 Fr. Rent for the Boichaille field 75 Fr. Inheritance taxes paid to Fabre, att. 2950 Fr., 1900 from the cash box, the rest from my bank account (withdrew 1500 Fr., 1050 of which I added to the 1900, and put 450 back in the cash box. Sawing of the poplar cut last January 85 Fr. Snowfall during the evening and all night long, in the morning there were 40 cm., the roof of the leanto next to the woodshed collapsed. Repairs for the clock in the salon 21 Fr.) the pages, the columns of figures and descriptions extending, rising, accumulating in a kind of patient tomb constructed stone by stone, as if some legal arrangements, some meddlesome and interfering administration only allowed our exhausted bones to he down at last in order to return to the original dust after having erected this kind of fabulous mausoleum consist¬ ing of time heaped upon a few ashes: ashes, nothingness, and on top, a pinnacle of vacancy in or upon which the ghosts of actions performed appear with a grim insignifi¬ cance, made concrete not by those ambitious inscriptions written on tombstones but by the absurd symbols of money, in a debased coinage which conferred upon the 118 old account books, as upon the actions of Balzac's heroes, that sort of falacious, laughable, and tiny unreality at the heart of which generals, bankers, countesses, and prosti¬ tutes seem to struggle and scratch each other's eyes out for the sake of a handful of pennies rattling in a street arab's pocket. So: the old woman-—the old, fragile heap of bones, skin, exhausted organs yearning for rest, for the original noth¬ ingness, lying—barely raising the sheet—at the heart, at the center of the house, reigning, invisible and omnipres¬ ent, not only over all the rooms (presiding—without needing any grace said—-at meals, at the common breaking of bread in the familiar clatter of plates, together, during the other old woman's ridiculous chatter), but even transcending these, extending her presence, her realm, beyond the walls, even beyond the death rattle, as if this need not even be noticed by the ear to be discerned at the foot of the hill, and even farther, now, in the silent night, the nocturnal peace of the garden, of the branches and the birds sleeping now, of the insects in the black grass, beneath the black sky scarcely lighter there where the twilight had just disappeared, as if out of a wound the light was slowly seeping through. And: the man-mountain, or rather the misshapen mass within which the old man was imprisoned, as though muzzled, immured in his own flesh, this same flesh busy feeding itself (or rather destroying itself: as if by the effect of a facetious malediction, of an imbecile and 119 mortal revenge of matter, the natural act—of digesting food—destined to maintain life now concluded in a result somehow inverse: its slow strangulation by its very excess), the hand holding the spoon, then the fork, accomplishing its function without, apparently, bothering with the mind's assent, the way an idiot, a child is fed: by surprise, with¬ out his knowing it, by force, the spoon or the fork some¬ times obliged to wait, patiently held near the mouth, inserting liquid or solid matter by somehow taking advan¬ tage of moments of inattention, that is, when the stare diminished, waned, fixed now not on Georges but on the hands with the long, thin, tapering fingers, a pianist's hands, his mother said, and paradoxically sunburnt, soiled, grease-stained, darkly silhouetted against the white table¬ cloth, incongruous, unexpected, their nails not merely dirty but edged all the way around with a black half-circle, the wrinkles of the skin encrusted with an indelible filth apparently consisting half of dust and half of oil closely mixed, having assumed that character not of a living tissue but of a hybrid substance—deriving both from the animal and mineral kingdoms—like the skin of peasants' hands or mechanics' hands, just as the lean, emaciated face that seemed to postulate beneath it a tie and white shirtfront surmounted, instead—it, too, sunburnt and soiled—the shapeless shirt and the overalls. Contemplating then (through those two unique and absurd fissures, the eyes, which probably permitted his mind to escape, to slip away—as if it too were forced to 120 act by ruse, clandestinely, to take advantage, so to speak, of a cleft, a fault in the substance—outside the monstrous prison of flesh, with a kind of lassitude, a perplexity, a musing incredulity) this person he probably had to admit he had engendered, that is, drawn from the original noth¬ ingness, created starting from zero (a contact of skin, an excitation of gland, an itching, an orgasm) and by an act if not voluntary in any case well-tried, projecting outside himself in a spasm (like, comparable to, a brief death, a sudden annihilation: actually a momentary eclipse of that piercing consciousness, as if that consciousness stopped existing during the interval corresponding to that parcel of itself which was separated in a terrible rending which results from a paroxysm of pleasure or perhaps—we are not certain—of pain—since, moreover, it also seems that at this very moment there is a confusion, the ejaculation being experienced simultaneously by the flesh and the mind as a kind of vague paroxysm, an explosion lighting up the brain at the same time as the obscure and red night of the womb, apparently related to those original myths of Gigantomachia in which creatures with the names (Uranus, Saturn) and dimensions of worlds couple, strug¬ gle fiercely against the night-blue background of the still starless heavens, and the male monster, frustrated in his desire, his giant conquest suddenly withdrawing with a twist of her loins, the seed spreading, a pollen polluting, infecting our mother the earth, immediately sowing before our horrified eyes a cursed progeniture), projecting outside 121 himself, then, a part of himself destined to survive him, that is to perpetuate him and therefore, ultimately, a prolongation of himself, even if it was apparently his negation, his adversary, and so, again, forced to recognize himself in it, so that contemplating those peasant's hands exposed, exhibited in the bright light (the lampshade of the wired oil lamp defining a luminous disc extending just beyond the table, the four people sitting around it remain¬ ing in the shadow, dark silhouettes, as if they were rele¬ gated to a background while against the dazzling white¬ ness of the tablecloth their hands and forearms seemed somehow detached from them), it was ultimately his own hands he was contemplating (and therefore those of his own father, similarly encrusted with—if not, as one might think at first glance, constituted of—dirt, and thin, not-too delicate, not tapering (that was probably the contribution of the undulating, unreal woman in the old photographs wearing her convolvulus dresses), but with that same fleshless quality—the fingers like dry sticks, the joints like knots), thinking perhaps (still immured in his stifling prison of flesh, not a muscle in his face moving save those necessary for mastication, and while his body busied itself, engaged itself, entirely absorbed—blind, voracious—in the action of eating, he seemed to be deprived of life, merely a mound of dead matter, all the agility, all the movement, all the sudden vitality of those sudden appearances and vanishings, those sudden accelerations and slackenings, concentrated in the motionless, fixed, heavy and somber 122 stare beneath the eyelids with their heavy folds): “My own self . . . thinking perhaps at the same moment, able to ” see in the same glance his own pudgy and even swollen hand, bones, joints and knuckles drowned, invisible be¬ neath the soft layer of fat, so that he couldn't even tell how it was made, if it resembled that other hand, this white, smooth skin which had never—or at least not for so long—touched, been in contact with anything but books, a hand lacking in reality and consistency as the air, the light—, and thinking: “All right. But what is it?" and per¬ haps even: “Maybe it's a law, a doom," then perhaps the rebellion, the rage: “No. No, I won't . . . ," and at that moment Sabine, who had not stopped watching him out of the corner of her eye the whole time she was talking, becoming even more voluble, the tone of her voice still rising, as if that voice could constitute a barrage, a ram¬ part, pretending (foreseeing, preparing for, hoping to deflect) anger even though she knew not only that none of the others was listening to her but even that they knew she knew it, not even bothering to assume an expression of pretending not to know it (Georges had started to eat again, his head bending over his plate once more with that gluttony or rather that affectation of gluttony which seemed superimposed, borrowed, assumed, just as the dirt and grease stains or even the sunburn seemed assumed, not in harmony with his too-pale hair, his lean, frail ap¬ pearance, Louise staring straight ahead of her as if she didn't notice that while she was still talking Sabine had 123
